argument: The Renaissance grew out of the trauma of the Black Death, which shattered the social and religious certainties of the High Middle Ages and pushed thinkers to look backward for models of renewal, much like the Warring States period in China or the Hellenistic age in Greece. Erasmus embodies this new humanism, arguing that centuries of scholastic fusion of faith and reason had let institutional power and doctrinal cleverness bury Christianity's simple ethical core, and that true spirituality is a personal, individual relationship with God centered on loving one another.
keyIdeas: The Dark Ages and Renaissance are oversimplified labels; the Middle Ages saw real prosperity, and progress can be measured in many ways besides intellectual advancement.
The Black Death killed 30-60% of Europe's population, triggering an economic and political crisis (peasant wage demands, wage freezes, revolt) that in turn produced an intellectual upheaval.

Erasmus's humanism blamed the centuries-long scholastic project of fusing Christian doctrine with Platonic/Aristotelian reason for letting institutional power and doctrinal cleverness eclipse the ethical core of religion.
Erasmus rejects the Socratic claim that ignorance is misery, arguing ignorance is simply the natural, common condition all humans are born into.

Erasmus's positive account of happiness is self-acceptance ('a person is ready to be what he is'), replacing both scholastic rationalism and elaborate ascetic ritual with a personal relationship to God centered on loving one another.
